documented_patterns_on_the_page.title: When a deal ended or changed, the company sued the state
documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: Foreign companies that bought or ran privatized water, gas and power services, or held mining rights, have used investment treaties to sue governments that froze tariffs, changed contracts, took services back or stopped a deal, including when protests forced it. Most of these claims went to ICSID, the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes in Washington, which its own website calls "one of the five organizations of the World Bank Group". The legal basis was usually a bilateral investment treaty, an agreement between two countries that lets a company from one sue the other.

documented_patterns_on_the_page.title: Aid money that goes back to companies in the donor country
documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary:
Tied aid is aid that must be spent on goods or services from the country that gave it. Eurodad, a European network of groups working on debt and aid, counted about $26.9 billion of tied aid in 2018, or 21% of bilateral and EU aid. Its total for formal and informal tying together is at least $32.3 billion and possibly up to $37.9 billion. It puts the direct short-term cost of tying at $2 billion to $7 billion.

documented_patterns_on_the_page.title: Funds that buy old debt and sue in New York and London
documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary:
When a country cannot pay, most lenders usually accept a reduced deal. A holdout refuses and sues for the full amount. A vulture fund is the critics' name for a fund that buys defaulted debt to do this. An ECB working paper (no. 2135, 2018) by Schumacher, Trebesch and Enderlein counted 158 cases against 34 defaulting governments from 1976 to 2010: 130 in US courts (82.3%), 23 in the UK (14.6%) and 5 in arbitration. New York law governs almost half of outstanding sovereign bonds (White & Case, 2024) or over 50% (Insurance Journal, 2026).

documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: The Paris Club is an informal group of creditor governments, dating to 1956, that reschedules loans together, case by case and tied to an IMF-backed programme. documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary:
Foreign direct investment earns income for its owners, and part stays in the host country. Globally in 2011, nearly one-third stayed in host economies and two-thirds went back to investors.

documented_patterns_on_the_page.summary: UNCTAD said in 2015 that about 30% of cross-border corporate investment passes through offshore hubs, and estimated developing countries lose about $100 billion a year in tax on investment linked to those hubs. IMF economists Damgaard, Elkjaer and Johannesen wrote in 2019 that phantom investment, money passing through empty companies, comes to $15 trillion, almost 40% of global FDI, up from about 30% less than a decade earlier. hyps.title: Lenders kept funding dictators they knew were stealing
hyps.conviction: Two leaked internal documents show lenders knew of large-scale theft; lending continued in both cases. How often this happened is the suspicion.
story: In 1982 a confidential report by a retired German central banker leaked from Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo. Erwin Blumenthal had been sent by the IMF to run the country's central bank, and on Zaire's $4.1 billion foreign debt he wrote that there was "no - I repeat no - chance" the creditors would be repaid, because of the corruption of the people in power. The lending did not stop. Probe International counted that over the next six years the IMF lent Zaire $600 million, the World Bank $650 million and Western governments nearly $3 billion, and when Mobutu Sese Seko was overthrown in 1997 the country owed more than $13 billion. The suspicion is that this was a habit, not an accident: that the big lenders often knew the governments they lent to were stealing, kept lending because those governments were useful allies, and then held ordinary people responsible for the debt.

Indonesia under Suharto is the second case on paper. In August 1997 World Bank staff in Jakarta wrote a confidential memo estimating that at least 20 to 30 per cent of the government's development budget was diverted through informal payments to officials and politicians, that there was no basis to claim Bank projects lost less, and that there were reports of 50 to 80 per cent being taken from money meant for land purchase and resettlement. The month before, the Bank's vice-president for East Asia, Jean-Michel Severino, had said the Bank knew exactly where its money was going. The memo became public only when the Wall Street Journal obtained it in 1998.

The Philippines shows who pays. Under Ferdinand Marcos, Westinghouse built the Bataan nuclear plant, which cost about $2.3 billion, was finished in 1984 and never produced electricity. Westinghouse admitted paying $17.2 million to a Marcos associate, Herminio Disini, which it called a legitimate commission, and a US jury acquitted the company of bribery in 1993. In 2021 the Philippine Supreme Court held Disini liable for using undue influence to win Westinghouse the contract. Filipinos finished paying the plant's loans in April 2007, a total of 64.7 billion pesos in principal and interest. There is an old idea in international law, odious debt, that debts a regime takes on against its own people should not bind them, but it has rarely been applied.

Lenders do not have to publish what their staff knew when a loan was approved, and the two documents above surfaced only through leaks. What would settle the suspicion are the internal country risk assessments and board papers for lending to Zaire, Indonesia and the Philippines in those years, and to other long-ruling allies, many of which are now old enough to request from the lenders' archives.
hyps.missing: No systematic review of lender archives for internal warnings of theft before continued lending.
hyps.would_settle: Internal country risk assessments and board papers for lending to Zaire, Indonesia and the Philippines in the 1970s to 1990s, requested from the World Bank and IMF archives.

hyps.title: The lenders expect the riots their conditions cause
hyps.conviction: A leaked World Bank strategy, a count of 146 protests and a global study linking adjustment loans to repression. Whether the lenders plan for repression is the suspicion.
story: On 25 June 2024 Kenya's parliament passed a finance bill full of new taxes, and protesters forced their way into the parliament building. Police opened fire. Kenya's state-funded human rights commission later said police had killed at least 60 people. Human Rights Watch reported that the bill was meant to raise an extra $2.3 billion, in part to meet IMF revenue requirements. The suspicion is that the lenders know, before they set conditions like these, that prices will rise, people will protest and governments will use force, and that they write this into their plans as an acceptable cost.

There is a paper trail. In 2001 Joseph Stiglitz, a former World Bank chief economist, described the "IMF riot" to the reporter Greg Palast as one of the steps of a lending programme. Palast's team at the Observer and the BBC obtained confidential World Bank documents, among them an interim strategy for Ecuador which said, more than once, that the plans could be expected to spark social unrest, and which called for meeting it with political resolve.

Researchers have counted what follows. In their 1994 book Free Markets and Food Riots, John Walton and David Seddon listed 146 protests against austerity in 39 debtor countries between 1976 and 1992. A global study by Rodwan Abouharb and David Cingranelli covering 1981 to 2000, which allowed for the fact that troubled countries are more likely to get such loans in the first place, found that carrying out a World Bank structural adjustment agreement worsened governments' respect for freedom from torture, political imprisonment, killings by the state and disappearances. This map holds cases of the same shape: the Caracazo in Venezuela in 1989, where the card counts 276 dead after fuel prices rose, and Ecuador in October 2019, where ending fuel subsidies more than doubled prices and 11 people died. The documented pattern on this map, the money kept flowing after the killings, shows that the lending usually continued.

The planning documents are usually confidential, and the Ecuador strategy came out through a leak. Lenders do not count deaths that follow their programmes. What would settle the question is a count across published IMF staff reports and World Bank programme documents of how often the risk sections predicted unrest before a big price rise, and whether the plan changed when they did. Many of those documents are now public after the fact, so the count can be done.
hyps.missing: No count of risk sections in IMF and World Bank programme documents that forecast unrest.
hyps.would_settle: A count of IMF staff reports and World Bank programme documents whose risk sections forecast unrest before major price increases, with whether the programme changed.

countries.note: At least 60 killed by police, per the national human rights commission.

hyps.title: Rescue money timed to keep friendly governments in power
hyps.conviction: Three rescues arrived just before elections, with one US official's reported admission and one president's public condition. Whether this is a regular practice is the suspicion.
story: In February 1996 the IMF agreed a $10.2 billion loan to Boris Yeltsin's government in Russia, four months before Yeltsin faced the Communist candidate, Gennady Zyuganov, in a presidential election in which he was trailing in the polls. The IMF's managing director said the Fund was not taking sides; Zyuganov called the loan political. That summer The Economist claimed that the IMF and the Russian government had worked together to keep Russia within the loan conditions on paper, and once Yeltsin had won, the IMF held back a payment. The suspicion is that the biggest powers behind the lenders time and size rescue money to keep friendly governments in office. If so, voters in borrowing countries are choosing under pressure they may not see.

Argentina has been through it twice. In June 2018 the IMF approved the largest loan in its history for the government of Mauricio Macri, raised in October to $57 billion, equal to 1,227 per cent of Argentina's quota at the Fund, a year before Macri ran for re-election. In July 2020 Mauricio Claver-Carone, Donald Trump's adviser on Latin America, was reported to have told a teleconference held by the Chilean Council on Foreign Relations that Trump asked the IMF for the loan so that Macri would win; Argentine senators repeated the account in a letter that November. The IMF's own 2021 review found the programme did not meet its objectives, only four of its twelve planned reviews were completed, and Macri lost. On 14 October 2025, twelve days before Argentina's midterm elections, Trump sat beside President Javier Milei at the White House, talked about the $20 billion the US Treasury had just made available, and said: "If he loses, we are not going to be generous with Argentina." His Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, said the support was tied to policy, not to the election. Milei's party won about 41 per cent of the vote.

Researchers have measured the tilt. A study of 157 countries from 1999 to 2005 by the economist Axel Dreher and colleagues found that countries voting with the United States at the UN General Assembly received lower inflation forecasts from the IMF as their elections approached. This map's documented pattern on aid and UN votes shows the same pull on aid.

The instructions that the US Treasury gives its director on the IMF board are not published, and board minutes are confidential for years. What would settle the question are those instructions and minutes for the 1996 and 2018 loans, and a count across all IMF programmes of approvals and payments in the months before elections, set against how closely each government votes with the largest shareholders.
hyps.missing: No count of IMF approvals and disbursements before elections, split by political alignment with major shareholders.
hyps.would_settle: US Treasury voting instructions and IMF board minutes for the 1996 Russian and 2018 Argentine arrangements; a count of pre-election approvals and disbursements across all IMF programmes by voting alignment.

hyps.title: Markets forced open for rich countries' subsidized food
hyps.conviction: A former US president's apology, a reversed tariff in Ghana and the collapse of local farming in both. Whether lending conditions are written for rich-country exporters is the suspicion.
story: In March 2010, two months after the earthquake that destroyed much of Port-au-Prince, Bill Clinton told the US Senate that a policy he had pushed in Haiti in the 1990s had been a mistake. "It may have been good for some of my farmers in Arkansas," he said, but it had cost Haiti its ability to grow its own rice. In 1995, under a programme run with the IMF and the World Bank, Haiti had cut its tariff on imported rice to 3 per cent, a year after Clinton restored President Jean-Bertrand Aristide to power. Haiti now buys more than 80 per cent of its rice from the United States, and between 1995 and 2011, according to the Environmental Working Group, Arkansas farmers received more than $2 billion in direct federal payments, half of it for rice. The suspicion is that conditions telling poor countries to cut tariffs on food imports were written to open markets for farm exporters in rich countries, whose governments pay them large subsidies, and that local farmers paid the price.

Ghana tells the same story with chickens. Imports of chicken rose from 26,000 tonnes in 2002 to about 40,000 tonnes in 2004, and local farmers' share of their own market fell from 95 per cent in 1992 to 11 per cent in 2002. In 2003 Ghana's parliament voted to double the tariff on imported poultry to 40 per cent. The government backed down within two months, under pressure from the IMF according to press reports, and Inter Press Service reported that the European Union's trade commissioner, Pascal Lamy, had lobbied against the tariff. The EU pays its own farmers about €43 billion a year.

Food aid follows the same direction. The long-running US food aid programme Food for Peace requires that the food it sends be grown in the United States, so emergency help sent through it is bought from American farmers and shipped. This map's documented pattern on tied aid shows how much aid money goes back to companies in the donor country.

The loan conditions are public; the reasons behind them are not. What would settle the question is a country-by-country comparison of the food-tariff cuts written into IMF and World Bank programmes with which rich countries' exporters gained market share afterwards, read beside the negotiating records, such as the instructions the US and EU gave their directors on those programmes.
hyps.missing: No country-by-country comparison of lender-required tariff cuts with subsequent export gains by rich-country suppliers.
hyps.would_settle: Food-tariff conditions in IMF and World Bank programmes matched to post-programme import shares by supplier country, read with US and EU instructions to their executive directors.

hyps.title: Spying on poor countries to win resource and trade deals
hyps.conviction: Australia's bugging of Timor-Leste's cabinet was exposed by the intelligence officer who led it, who later pleaded guilty to revealing secret information, and was followed by a renegotiated treaty, though Australia has never officially confirmed it; the Snowden files show spying on G20 delegates and Brazil's state oil company. That rich governments routinely spy to win economic deals is the suspicion.
story: In 2004 a team from Australia's foreign intelligence service, ASIS, placed listening devices in the walls of Timor-Leste's cabinet offices in Dili, which were being renovated under an Australian aid project. Timor-Leste was one of the poorest countries in the region, two years independent, and it was negotiating with Australia over how to share the oil and gas of the Timor Sea, including the Greater Sunrise fields. ABC's Lateline reported that transcripts of the bugged conversations were delivered to Australia's negotiating team. The treaty signed in 2006 split Greater Sunrise's revenue evenly and set no permanent border. The operation came out years later through a former ASIS officer, known only as Witness K. Timor-Leste took Australia to arbitration in The Hague in 2013, and in 2018 the two countries signed a new treaty setting a maritime boundary. Witness K pleaded guilty to conspiring to reveal secret information and received a suspended sentence; the prosecution of his lawyer, Bernard Collaery, was dropped in July 2022. The suspicion is that rich governments routinely spy on poorer ones to win resource and trade deals, and that the deals people later live under were negotiated by one side that could hear the other's plans.

The Snowden files show the same thing at larger meetings. In 2013 the Guardian reported documents showing that Britain's signals intelligence agency, GCHQ, had intercepted the phones and computers of delegates at the G20 meetings in London in 2009, including by setting up internet cafes for them, and had passed what it gathered to British ministers. Among the targets it named was the Turkish finance minister. The same year Brazil's TV Globo reported documents showing that the US National Security Agency had targeted Petrobras, Brazil's state oil company, through a programme that extracts data from private networks. Brazil's president, Dilma Rousseff, said that if confirmed it could only be for economic and strategic reasons.
Spying of this kind is generally authorized under the spying country's own law, so it is rarely tried in that country's courts, and the people who reveal it are often the ones prosecuted.

What would settle how common it is are the intelligence agencies' records of operations against trade, debt and resource negotiations, which only a leak or a court order is likely to produce. Short of that, a count of negotiations later reopened or challenged on the ground of spying, as Timor-Leste did, would show whether the known cases are rare or merely the ones that surfaced.
hyps.missing: No count of trade, debt or resource negotiations reopened on espionage grounds.
hyps.would_settle: Intelligence records of operations against economic negotiations, obtained by leak or court order; a count of negotiations reopened or challenged on espionage grounds.

hyps.title: Foreign advisers who profit from the privatisations they design
hyps.conviction: A US court found Harvard's lead advisers on Russia's privatisation liable for investing on the side; the loans-for-shares auctions are widely described as rigged. That advisers and insiders routinely profit from sell-offs they shape is the suspicion.
story: In December 1992 the US aid agency, USAID, hired the Harvard Institute for International Development to advise Boris Yeltsin's government on turning Russia's state economy into a market one, a contract eventually worth tens of millions of dollars. The project's leaders, the Harvard economist Andrei Shleifer and the lawyer Jonathan Hay, were meant to be neutral advisers. In 2004 a US federal judge found both liable under the US False Claims Act for making personal investments in Russia while advising on its markets, including shares in Russian oil companies held in the name of Shleifer's father-in-law. In 2005 Harvard paid $26.5 million to settle, Shleifer agreed to pay $2 million and Hay up to $2 million, none of them admitting liability, and the institute had already been dissolved. The suspicion is that the foreign advisers and favoured insiders who design the sale of a country's public assets routinely position themselves to profit from it, so that the advice is shaped by who will buy.

Russia's next large sell-off went to insiders. In November and December 1995 the government ran the loans-for-shares auctions, in which stakes in 12 large state companies, including Norilsk Nickel and the oil company Yukos, were pledged to banks in return for loans to the state. The banks that ran the auctions won most of them, usually for bids just above the starting price; 51 per cent of the voting shares in Norilsk Nickel went for about $170 million and 45 per cent of Yukos for about $159 million. Contemporary reports described the auctions as rigged, and the scheme gave several of the men later called the oligarchs control of major companies. Some economists, such as Daniel Treisman, argue that the companies were later run better than comparable state firms. On this map, a Lancet study links Russia's mass privatisation to a sharp rise in deaths among working-age men.

The advisers' own investments came out after American whistle-blowers in Moscow complained and the US government sued. Advisory contracts on privatisation are usually confidential, and there is no public register of what the advisers, their firms or their families hold in the companies being sold.

What would settle it is a comparison, for large privatisations financed or advised by foreign lenders, of who designed the sale against who bought into it, using the advisory contracts and the shareholder registers that followed. If advisers and their associates turn up among the buyers more often than chance, the suspicion holds.
hyps.missing: No comparison of privatisation advisers against later shareholders across lender-advised sales.
hyps.would_settle: Advisory contracts for large lender-advised privatisations matched against subsequent shareholder registers.

hyps.title: Development money that flows through tax havens
hyps.conviction: Oxfam found most of the World Bank's private-sector lending in sub-Saharan Africa went to companies using tax havens. That development lenders are helping the companies they fund avoid the taxes the countries need is the suspicion.
story: In April 2016, days after the Panama Papers broke, Oxfam published an analysis of the companies that the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank's lending arm for private business, had funded in sub-Saharan Africa in 2015. Of the 68 companies, 51 used tax havens in ways that had no apparent link to their business, and together they received 84 per cent of the money the IFC put into the region that year. Mauritius was the most common haven, involved in 40 per cent of the IFC's projects in the region. The IFC's investments in companies using havens had more than doubled in five years, from $1.2 billion in 2010 to $2.87 billion in 2015. The suspicion is that the development lenders, whose stated purpose is to help poor countries raise their own money, are funding the very corporate structures that drain those countries of tax.

This map's documented pattern on investment routed through tax havens records UNCTAD's estimate that developing countries lose about $100 billion a year in tax on investment linked to offshore hubs, and the IMF economists' finding that almost 40 per cent of global foreign direct investment passes through empty companies, mostly in ten economies including Mauritius. Senegal ended its tax treaty with Mauritius in 2020, saying it had cost $257 million in lost revenue.

The IFC said in response that there are legitimate uses for offshore structures and that it requires the companies it funds to comply with tax law. But the IFC does not publish how much tax its clients pay in the countries where they operate, and its disclosure rules do not require clients to show it, so whether the havens are being used to cut tax cannot be checked from outside.

What would settle it is country-by-country reporting of profits and taxes paid by every company that development lenders fund, set beside where those companies are incorporated. If the companies booking profits in havens pay markedly less tax in the countries where they operate, the suspicion holds.
hyps.missing: No country-by-country tax reporting for development-lender clients.
hyps.would_settle: Country-by-country profit and tax reporting by all companies funded by development lenders, compared by place of incorporation.

countries.note: Linked to 40 per cent of IFC projects in sub-Saharan Africa in 2015.

hyps.title: Western banks that knowingly hold money stolen from poor countries
hyps.conviction: A US Senate inquiry and a guilty plea showed Riggs Bank serving Equatorial Guinea's ruler; Britain's regulator found 15 banks with serious failings over Abacha's money; the FinCEN Files show major banks moving $2 trillion they had flagged as suspicious. That big banks routinely take such money because it pays is the suspicion.
story: In July 2004 a US Senate investigations subcommittee reported on Riggs Bank, a Washington bank that held accounts for more than 95 per cent of the foreign embassies in the city. Its single largest customer was the government and ruling family of Equatorial Guinea, a small West African country where oil had been found but most people stayed poor. From 1995 Riggs held more than 60 accounts for the government, President Teodoro Obiang Nguema, his relatives and officials, with balances of up to $700 million. The subcommittee found that Riggs had helped set up offshore shell companies for the president and his sons, accepted nearly $13 million in cash deposits into accounts controlled by the president and his wife, some of it carried in by suitcase, and let more than $35 million be wired from government accounts to companies it had reason to think the president controlled. US regulators fined Riggs $25 million in 2004, and in January 2005 it pleaded guilty to failing to report suspicious transactions and paid a further $16 million. The prosecutor said Riggs had aggressively cultivated the accounts despite repeated warnings. The suspicion is that large Western banks regularly take and move money stolen from the public of poor countries, because it is profitable, and treat the occasional fine as a cost of business.

Britain found the same thing with Nigeria. After the death in 1998 of General Sani Abacha, whose regime was estimated to have taken at least $5 billion, Britain's Financial Services Authority looked at how London banks had handled his family's money. In 2001 it reported 42 accounts linked to the Abacha family and associates at 23 banks, with $1.3 billion passing through them between 1996 and 2000, 98 per cent of it at 15 banks with significant control weaknesses. The regulator did not name the banks, and none was prosecuted.

In September 2020 the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and BuzzFeed News published the FinCEN Files, more than 2,100 reports that banks had filed with the US Treasury about transactions they suspected. Between 1999 and 2017 the banks had flagged more than $2 trillion in payments, and the leak showed that five global banks, JPMorgan Chase, HSBC, Standard Chartered, Deutsche Bank and Bank of New York Mellon, kept moving money for suspect clients even after being fined for earlier failures. Banks can stop a suspicious payment but often are not required to; filing a report is often enough. A report is not in itself evidence of wrongdoing; the banks denied systematic wrongdoing, and FinCEN, the Treasury agency that receives the reports, condemned the leak.

What would settle the scale of it is the full set of suspicious-activity reports and the bank records behind them, which are secret by law, together with a count of how many accounts of senior officials from poor countries banks keep after flagging them. Only leaks and occasional inquiries have shown any of it.
hyps.missing: No count of politically exposed accounts kept open after being flagged as suspicious.
hyps.would_settle: Suspicious-activity reports and underlying records for accounts of senior officials from low-income countries, with what banks did after flagging them.

hyps.title: Debt-for-nature deals that hand oceans and forests to foreign financiers
hyps.conviction: Ecuador's and Belize's swaps were funded by bonds Credit Suisse arranged, with binding conservation terms, and private members hold six of eleven seats on Ecuador's Galápagos fund; Galápagos groups complained to the IDB over lack of information. That these deals serve bankers and foreign conservation groups more than the countries is the suspicion.
story: In May 2023 Ecuador announced what was called the largest debt-for-nature swap in history. Credit Suisse, the Swiss bank, bought back $1.63 billion of Ecuador's bonds from investors at between 35.5 and 53.25 cents on the dollar, after a political crisis had driven their price down. To pay for it, a company set up in Ireland, GPS Blue Financing, sold $656 million of new 'Galápagos marine bonds' to investors and lent the money to Ecuador. Because the US government's development bank insured the deal and the Inter-American Development Bank guaranteed part of it, Moody's rated the new bonds Aa2, among its highest grades, while Ecuador's own bonds were rated junk. In return Ecuador committed to spend about $12 million a year on marine conservation in the Galápagos for almost two decades, through a new fund, the Galápagos Life Fund, on whose 11-member board, according to the Latin American network Latindadd, six seats went to private and non-government members. In 2024 Galápagos community groups complained to the Inter-American Development Bank's watchdog that they had been given too little information and no say; the finance ministry did not provide all the financial documents a local rights group requested. The suspicion is that these swaps, sold as debt relief for nature, are designed around the fees and safe returns of bankers and the control of foreign conservation groups, with small savings for the country and decisions over its own waters and forests moved outside its government.

Belize's deal in 2021 set the model. A subsidiary of the US charity The Nature Conservancy lent Belize the money to buy back its $553 million 'superbond' at 55 cents on the dollar, funded by bonds Credit Suisse arranged and insured by the US development bank. In return Belize legally committed to protect 30 per cent of its ocean by 2026, up from 15.9 per cent, and to spend about $4 million a year on marine conservation until 2041, with higher payments if it misses the targets. Belize's debt fell by about a tenth of its national income.

Similar deals followed in Barbados, Gabon, the Bahamas and, in 2024, Ecuador's Amazon. In January 2023 Barclays questioned in a note to investors whether such swaps deserve their green label, since only a small part of the money raised reaches conservation; other critics point to the arrangers' fees and the cost of the insurance, neither fully published. Credit Suisse, which arranged the largest, collapsed and was taken over by UBS in 2023.

What would settle it is publication of the full terms of each swap: fees and insurance premiums, what the country saved after all costs, who sits on each conservation fund and what they can decide, and what local communities were told before signing. Ecuador's Galápagos papers were requested under freedom-of-information law and not all were released.
hyps.missing: Full fees, insurance costs and net savings of each swap are not published.
hyps.would_settle: Published fees, insurance premiums, net fiscal savings and governance rules for each debt-for-nature swap, with records of local consultation.

hyps.title: Private tribunals that can order countries to pay companies billions
hyps.conviction: Investor-state tribunals have ordered Pakistan to pay $5.9 billion and Ecuador $1.77 billion; a study found 15 arbitrators decided 55% of known cases. That the system is run by a small club of lawyers that favours investors and deters governments from regulating is the suspicion.
story: On 12 July 2019 a tribunal at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, part of the World Bank Group, ordered Pakistan to pay $5.976 billion to Tethyan Copper, a company owned by the Canadian miner Barrick Gold and Chile's Antofagasta. Pakistan's province of Balochistan refused Tethyan a lease in November 2011 to mine Reko Diq, one of the world's largest untouched copper and gold deposits, and in 2013 Pakistan's Supreme Court declared the original deal void. The tribunal held that Pakistan had treated the company unfairly and awarded $4.087 billion for the mine's value plus interest and costs, a sum equal to about 2 per cent of Pakistan's national income and almost the size of the $6 billion loan the IMF had just agreed to lend Pakistan. Reuters reported that the company had invested more than $220 million in the project; its owners have put their spending at more than $500 million. In 2022 Pakistan settled: the award was dropped, Barrick took 50 per cent of a revived mine, and Pakistani state companies paid Antofagasta $900 million to leave. The suspicion is that the system of investor-state tribunals, written into thousands of investment treaties, lets foreign companies override national courts and laws in private hearings, run by a small group of lawyers who profit from the cases, so that poor countries pay billions or give in rather than regulate.

Ecuador was ordered in October 2012 to pay the American oil company Occidental $1.77 billion, $2.3 billion with interest, then the largest award in the centre's history, after Ecuador ended Occidental's contract for an Amazon oil block in 2006 because the company had transferred part of its stake to another firm without government approval, as the contract required. One of the three arbitrators dissented. In 2015 a review committee cut the award to about $1 billion, which Ecuador paid.

A 2012 study by Corporate Europe Observatory and the Transnational Institute, Profiting from Injustice, found that 15 arbitrators, nearly all from Europe, the United States or Canada, had decided 55 per cent of all known investment-treaty disputes, and that several prominent arbitrators had sat on the boards of multinational companies, including some that had sued developing countries. Arbitrators at the centre are paid by the hour, and the same lawyers often act as arbitrator in one case and as counsel in another. Defenders of the system point out that, by UNCTAD's count, states win more concluded cases than investors, about 38 per cent against 29 per cent, and that each side chooses one of the three arbitrators. This map's documented pattern on companies suing states counts the claims.

The awards are published only in some cases, and the cost to governments of laws never passed for fear of being sued cannot be seen at all. What would settle the question is full publication of every case, the arbitrators' financial ties to the companies and law firms involved, and a record of regulations that governments withdrew or weakened after a company threatened a claim.
hyps.missing: Not all awards are published; arbitrators' ties are not publicly disclosed; laws withdrawn under threat of claims are unrecorded.
hyps.would_settle: Full publication of all investor-state cases, arbitrators' financial ties, and a record of regulations withdrawn after threatened claims.
